petAge.title: Dog & Cat Age in Human Years
petAge.subtitle: Convert your dog's or cat's age to human years, see its life stage and checkup schedule, and get daily calories and food amounts on one screen. Based on AKC, AAHA and other veterinary sources.

input.title: Your pet
input.birthHint: Enter a birthday to set the age as of today.
input.birthErr: Enter a past date that makes the age {max} years or less.
input.weightHint: Use a recent weight. Daily calories are based on weight.
input.weightLoss: For weight loss, enter the target (ideal) weight instead of the current weight.
input.weightErr: Enter a weight between {min} and {max} kg.
input.sizeHint: {w} kg puts this dog in {size}. Pick another size if the breed standard differs.
input.kcalHint: Enter the metabolizable energy from the bag. The default {k} is a typical dry-food example. Divide kcal/kg by 10.
input.kcalErr: Enter food energy between {min} and {max} kcal/100g.

result.label: A {age} {pet} in human years
result.byDog: From the AKC chart for {size} dogs.
result.byCat: From the International Cat Care chart.

result.disclaimer: Age conversion and feeding amounts are general estimates. Breed and health change them, so talk to your veterinarian first.

stage.title: Life stage

dog.puppy: From birth until rapid growth ends, around 6–9 months depending on breed and size.
dog.young: From the end of rapid growth until physical and social maturity, which most dogs reach by 3–4 years.
dog.mature: From maturity (3–4 years) until the last 25% of the estimated lifespan begins.
dog.senior: The last 25% of the estimated lifespan.

stage.seniorDog: With an average {size}-dog lifespan of {lo}–{hi} years (AKC), senior starts at about {a}–{b} years.
stage.endOfLife: End-of-life can happen at any age, so it is not set by age here. Stage boundaries are the approximate ones in the AAHA guidelines.

puppy: Start deworming at 2 weeks and repeat every 2 weeks until year-round control begins.
Expect several fecal parasite tests (4) in the first year.
Set the core vaccine schedule with your veterinarian.
young: Baseline blood and urine tests now give you something to compare with later.
Weight gain is common after spay/neuter, so watch weight and body condition.
mature: Exams every 6–12 months, with basic blood and urine tests every year.
Tracking weight and body condition helps catch disease early.
senior: Exams at least every 6 months, with blood and urine tests every 6–12 months.
Mobility, vision, hearing and cognition may decline. Add traction on floors and cut down on stairs.

kitten: Every cat should see a veterinarian at least once a year.
This is the time to catch congenital problems early.
Kittens can start weaning onto kitten food at 3–5 weeks.
young: See a veterinarian at least once a year.
Preventing obesity matters most now. Neutered cats, especially males, gain weight easily.
mature: See a veterinarian at least once a year and watch for early kidney disease.
Daily energy needs may drop to about RER at this age. Adjust by weight.
senior: See a veterinarian at least every 6 months.
Being underweight is common in senior cats. They may need 10–20%, sometimes 25%, more than RER.

feed.title: Daily calories and food
feed.how: RER = 70 × {w} kg^0.75 = {rer} kcal, factor {f} ({name}), food {k} kcal/100g.
feed.rangeWhy: AAHA 2021 nutrition guidelines and the MSD Veterinary Manual list different factors, so a range is shown.
feed.treat: Keep treats within {kcal} kcal a day (10% of daily calories) and cut food by the same amount.
feed.vary: Pets of the same weight can need up to 30% more or fewer calories. Adjust by weight and body condition score (BCS).
feed.weaning: During weaning, milk or milk replacer is the main food and this calculation may not fit. Ask your veterinarian.
feed.lossNote: The weight-loss factor uses ideal weight. Make sure the weight field holds the target weight, and plan weight loss with your veterinarian.
feed.growthNote: Under 1 year uses growth factors, so spay/neuter and activity do not change daily calories.

note.dog: Ages 1–16 come from the AKC chart; ages 17–20 for small, medium and large come from the IDEXX (Fred L. Metzger) chart. * marks values not in the source, estimated from neighbors (under 1 year, giant 17+). The UCSD formula is a Labrador-based reference.

guide.title: Dog and cat age and feeding guide

howTo.title: How to use
items: Pick a species and enter the age (or birthday) and weight to see human age, life stage and daily food right away.
Dogs get a size (small, medium, large, giant) from their weight. Pick another size if the breed standard differs.
For food energy, enter the metabolizable energy on the bag (kcal/100g or kcal/kg). Divide kcal/kg by 10.
Use the share buttons under the result to get a link and image that reopen the same result.

method.title: How it is calculated
items: Dogs: the AKC size chart as published. Year 1 is 15 and year 2 is 24, then about 4–7 years per year depending on size (giant dogs: 12 and 22). Months are split evenly between whole years.

Puppies under 1 year are not in the chart, so values are estimated on a straight line from 0 at birth to the 1-year value. Past the end of the chart (giant 17+, over 20) the last yearly step is extended.
UCSD formula: human age = 16 × ln(dog age) + 31. It was built from Labrador retrievers, so it is shown only as a reference.
Cats: the International Cat Care chart. Year 1 is 15 and year 2 is 24, then 4 years per year, with monthly values before age 1.

Daily calories: RER = 70 × weight (kg)^0.75 and MER = RER × factor. Neutered adult dog 1.4–1.6, intact dog 1.6–1.8, neutered cat 1.2–1.4, intact cat 1.4–1.6, puppy under 4 months 3.0 then 2.0, kitten 2.5.
Daily food (g) = daily calories ÷ food energy (kcal/100g) × 100, and each meal = daily food ÷ meals per day.

tips.title: Good to know
items: Treat the numbers as a starting point. Pets of the same weight can need up to 30% more or fewer calories, so adjust by weight and body condition score (BCS).
Keep treats under 10% of daily calories and cut food by the same amount.
When losing weight, enter the target (ideal) weight, not the current weight. The weight-loss factor uses ideal weight.
Under 1 year uses growth factors. When growth ends depends on breed and size, so ask your veterinarian before switching food.

items.q: Why is '1 dog year = 7 human years' wrong?
items.a: Dogs and cats grow very fast in the first one or two years and then age slowly. On the AKC chart, 1 year is 15 human years and 2 years is 24, then each year adds 4–7 depending on size. Multiplying by 7 makes year 1 just 7 and year 2 just 14, which badly understates the early years and misses the size differences later on.

items.q: Do small dogs live longer than large dogs?
items.a: AKC lists average lifespans of 10–15 years for small breeds (some up to 18), 10–13 for medium, 8–12 for large and 8–10 for giant breeds. The age chart also spreads apart by size from age 6: at 10, a small dog is 56 in human years and a giant dog is 79. So senior age (the last 25% of lifespan) comes earlier for bigger dogs.

items.q: The amount on the food bag differs from this result.
items.a: How feeding guides on bags are made is not standardized (AAHA 2021), and pets of the same weight can need up to 30% more or fewer calories (MSD Veterinary Manual). Use either as a starting point and adjust by weight and body condition. Enter the energy value from the bag here to recalculate for your pet's weight.

items.q: How can I tell if my pet is overweight?
items.a: The WSAVA body condition score (BCS) runs from 1 to 9, with 4–5 ideal. Ribs are easy to feel under a thin fat layer, the waist is visible from above and the belly tucks up from the side. If the ribs are hard to feel and there is no waist, your pet is on the heavy side; set a target weight with your veterinarian.

items.q: When is a cat a senior?
items.a: The 2021 AAHA/AAFP guidelines use kitten up to 1 year, young adult 1–6 years, mature adult 7–10 years and senior over 10 years. They recommend checkups at least once a year for every cat and at least every 6 months for seniors. End-of-life can happen at any age.

items.q: Why does the UCSD formula differ from the chart?
items.a: The UCSD team (Wang et al., Cell Systems 2020) compared DNA methylation changes in about a hundred Labrador retrievers with humans and derived '16 × ln(dog age) + 31'. It makes year 1 equal 31 and year 5 equal 57, counting youth more heavily. Because it comes from one breed it may not fit other breeds or sizes, so it is shown only as a reference.

items.q: How many treats can I give?
items.a: The AAHA 2021 nutrition guidelines say complete and balanced food should make up at least 90% of daily calories, with treats and other foods 10% or less. Stay within the treat limit in the result and cut food by the same amount.

sources.title: Sources
sources.akcYears: AKC, How to Calculate Dog Years to Human Years (updated 2026-09-14) — size chart and weight classes
sources.idexx: IDEXX, How old is your pet in people years? (2016, Fred L. Metzger chart) — small/medium/large ages 17–20
sources.ucsd: Wang et al., Quantitative Translation of Dog-to-Human Aging by Conserved Remodeling of the DNA Methylome, Cell Systems (2020)
sources.icatcare: International Cat Care, Cat life stages — cat age chart
sources.aahaFeline: 2021 AAHA/AAFP Feline Life Stage Guidelines (JFMS 23:211–233) — cat life stages, visit frequency, senior energy needs
sources.aahaCanine: 2019 AAHA Canine Life Stage Guidelines (JAAHA 55:267–290) — dog life stages and checkups
sources.akcLifespan: AKC, How Long Do Dogs Live? (2021-05-27) — average lifespan by size
sources.aahaNutrition: 2021 AAHA Nutrition and Weight Management Guidelines for Dogs and Cats — RER, MER factors (Box 1), 10% treats
sources.msd: MSD Veterinary Manual, Daily Maintenance Energy Requirements for Dogs and Cats — MER factors
sources.wsavaBcs: WSAVA Global Nutrition Committee, Body Condition Score (Dog)
sources.method: Puppies under 1 year and ages past the end of a chart are not in the sources, so they are estimated on a straight line from neighboring values (marked * in the table). The default dry-food energy of 380 kcal/100g is an example value.
